# Multiple myeloma

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Hematology and oncology > White blood cell and bone marrow disorders > Multiple myeloma*

[Original Article Link](/library/5T0ir2)

---

## Summary

Multiple myeloma (MM) is a malignant <u>plasma cell dyscrasia</u> characterized by uncontrolled <u>proliferation</u> and diffuse infiltration of monoclonal <u>plasma cells</u> in the <u>bone marrow</u>. Malignant <u>plasma cells</u> produce <u>monoclonal proteins</u> (also known as <u>M proteins</u> or paraproteins) such as abnormal <u>immunoglobulins</u> (e.g., <u>IgG</u>, <u>IgA</u>) and <u>free light chains</u> (e.g., <u>Bence Jones proteins</u>). MM is more common in older adults and manifests with nonspecific symptoms (<u>fever</u>, night sweats, weight loss), <u>symptoms of hypercalcemia</u>, bone <u>pain</u>, and/or <u>back pain</u>. This condition is sometimes discovered incidentally in asymptomatic individuals. The <u>proliferation</u> of <u>plasma cells</u> suppresses normal <u>bone marrow</u> function, which may lead to <u>anemia</u>, bleeding, and/or infection. <u>Plasma cell</u> <u>proliferation</u> can also result in <u>osteolysis</u> and <u>hypercalcemia</u>. Renal complications are common, including <u>myeloma cast nephropathy</u>, <u>light chain</u> deposition disease, <u>amyloid light-chain (AL) amyloidosis</u> with renal involvement, and <u>nephrocalcinosis</u>. Most patients are treated with a combination of <u>high-dose chemotherapy</u> and <u>autologous stem cell transplantation</u>; patients with impaired functional status are treated with <u>chemotherapy</u> alone. While advancements in treatment regimens have resulted in improved patient outcomes, most patients with MM eventually relapse.

## Epidemiology

* Sex: : <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> (3:2) [[1]](/library/ETX8sx)

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: : 50–70 years  [[1]](/library/ETX8sx)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Classification

* Based on <u>immunoglobulin</u> type [[2]](/library/uTXpsx)

* <u>IgG</u> and <u>IgA</u>: typical multiple myeloma; majority of patients

* Bence Jones myeloma (<u>free light chains</u> excreted in urine): 15–20% of multiple myelomas

* <u>IgD</u>, <u>IgE</u>, and <u>IgM</u>: very rare subtypes of multiple myelomas

---

## Pathophysiology

* <u>Neoplastic</u> <u>proliferation</u> of <u>plasma cells</u>

* <u>Bone marrow</u> infiltration by malignant <u>plasma cells</u> → suppression of <u>hematopoiesis</u> → <u>leukopenia</u>, <u>thrombocytopenia</u>, <u>anemia</u>

* Cell <u>proliferation</u> → pro-osteoclastogenic factors (e.g., <u>TNF-α</u>, <u>IL-1</u>, <u>RANK</u>-L) → <u>osteolytic lesions</u> → <u>hypercalcemia</u>

* Overproduction of monoclonal <u>immunoglobulin</u> and/or <u>light chains</u> → dysproteinemia (a state of pathologically increased synthesis of <u>immunoglobulins</u> and/or their subunits) → <u>kidney</u> damage (e.g., <u>myeloma cast nephropathy</u>) and/or paraprotein tissue deposition (may cause <u>amyloidosis</u>) [[3]](/library/4kc3Lc0)[[4]](/library/kkcmLc0)

* Nonfunctioning <u>antibodies</u> → functional <u>antibody</u> deficiency

* ↑ Serum viscosity → <u>hyperviscosity syndrome</u>





![Multiple myeloma fact sheet](media/mog983hgrhjcdx22jl9cpe6k.jpg)

Multiple myeloma fact sheet

---

## Clinical features

* Often asymptomatic

* Mild <u>fever</u>, night sweats, <u>weakness</u>, and weight loss

* Bone <u>pain</u>, especially <u>back pain</u> (most common symptom)

* Symptoms of <u>hypercalcemia</u>

* Spontaneous <u>fractures</u>

* Increased risk of infection

* Increased risk of <u>petechial</u> bleeding

* Foamy urine (caused by <u>Bence Jones proteins</u> in urine)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Enlarged lymph nodes</u> are not a typical finding.

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[5]](/library/M11Mhf0)[[6]](/library/n117hf0)[[7]](/library/Qu1uIi0)




* Obtain a minimum diagnostic workup.

* Initial <u>laboratory studies</u> (e.g., <u>CBC</u>, <u>CMP</u>, <u>urinalysis</u>)

* <u>Myeloma biomarkers</u> (e.g., serum and urine protein <u>electrophoresis</u>, <u>free light chain</u> assay, <u>LDH</u>)

* Imaging to assess for bone lesions (e.g., whole-body <u>low-dose CT scan</u>)

* Refer to an oncologist for diagnostic confirmation via <u>bone marrow biopsy</u>.

* Evaluate for <u>diagnostic criteria of multiple myeloma</u>.

* Use the Revised International Staging System (R-ISS) to categorize the disease state.

* Consider differential diagnoses (e.g., other <u>plasma cell dyscrasias</u>; , other <u>causes of hypercalcemia</u> or bone lesions).





> [!TIP]
> Evaluation of a patient with suspected multiple myeloma (e.g., a patient with <u>CRAB criteria</u>) should include <u>CBC</u>, <u>CMP</u>, <u>immunoglobulin</u> studies, <u>LDH</u>, <u>β<sub>2</sub> microglobulin</u>, bone imaging, and a <u>bone marrow biopsy</u>.




### Diagnostic criteria




| <br>International Myeloma Working Group diagnostic criteria for multiple myeloma [[8]](/library/LgXwDx)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Criteria |  | Description |
| <u>Histopathology</u> |  | <br><br>* <u>Bone marrow biopsy</u> findings of ≥ 10% clonal <u>bone marrow</u> <u>plasma cells</u><br><br>* OR <u>biopsy</u>-proven <u>plasmacytoma</u> (bony or extramedullary)<br><br><br> |
| Myeloma defining events | <br><u>End-organ damage</u> (CRAB criteria)<br> | <br><br>* Calcium > 11 mg/dL or > 1 mg/dL above the <u>ULN</u><br><br>* Renal insufficiency: <u>GFR</u> < 40 mL/min or serum <u>creatinine</u> > 2 mg/dL<br><br>* Anemia: <u>Hb</u> < 10 g/dL or more than 2 g/dL below the <u>LLN</u><br><br>* Bone lesions: ≥ 1 <u>osteolytic lesions</u> on imaging<br><br><br> |
| Biomarkers of <u>malignancy</u> | <br><br>* ≥ 60% clonal <u>bone marrow</u> <u>plasma cells</u><br><br>* <u>SFLC</u> level ≥ 100 mg/L with an <u>involved:uninvolved SFLC ratio</u> ≥ 100<br><br>* > 1 focal skeletal lesion on <u>MRI</u> (â¥ 5 mm in size)<br><br><br> |  |
| <br><br>* Diagnosis of multiple myeloma:<br><br>* Histopathological criteria met<br><br>* AND ≥ 1 <u>myeloma defining event</u><br><br><br> |  |  |





> [!NOTE]
> <u>CRAB</u> criteria for organ damage due to a <u>plasma cell</u> disorder: Calcium increased, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, Bone lesions




> [!TIP]
> Evaluation for biomarkers of <u>malignancy</u> may allow for diagnosis and <u>treatment of multiple myeloma</u> before <u>end-organ damage</u> has occurred.




### Laboratory tests [[7]](/library/Qu1uIi0)[[8]](/library/LgXwDx)




#### Routine studies




* <u>CBC</u> (with differential and <u>peripheral smear</u>)

* <u>Anemia</u>, <u>thrombocytopenia</u>, and/or <u>leukopenia</u>

* <u>Decreased reticulocyte count</u>

* <u>Rouleaux formation</u>

* <u>CMP</u>

* Increased <u>creatinine</u>

* <u>Hypercalcemia</u>

* Elevated total protein with paraprotein (gamma) gap

* <u>Inflammatory markers</u>: Increased <u>ESR</u>

* <u>Urinalysis</u>: : may be negative for protein





![Rouleaux formation](media/pyp9fbrzuffjqpzd1pzgp3vd.jpg)

Rouleaux formation




#### Myeloma biomarkers




* Blood tests

* <u>Immunoglobulin</u> studies (common initial tests)

* <u>Serum protein electrophoresis</u> (<u>SPEP</u>): presence of <u>M protein</u> (<u>M spike</u>)

* <u>Serum protein</u> <u>immunofixation</u>: monoclonal gammopathy

* <u>Serum free light chain assay</u> (<u>SFLC</u>): increased κ or λ <u>light chains</u>, increased <u>SFLC involved:uninvolved ratio</u>

* Quantitative <u>immunoglobulin</u> levels (<u>IgA</u>, <u>IgG</u>, <u>IgM</u>) can help determine if proteinemia on <u>SPEP</u> is monoclonal.

* Increased <u>β<sub>2</sub> microglobulin</u> [[9]](/library/jUY_1o)

* Increased <u>LDH</u>

* Urine studies

* <u>Urine protein electrophoresis</u> (<u>UPEP</u>) with <u>immunofixation</u>

* Bence Jones proteins: monoclonal <u>immunoglobulin light chains</u> produced by <u>neoplastic</u> cells

* Bence Jones <u>proteinuria</u> is suggestive of <u>plasma cell</u> disorders (e.g., multiple myeloma, <u>Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia</u>).

* 24-hour urine protein and <u>creatinine</u>





![Multiple myeloma - serum protein electrophoresis with M protein](media/qzj5o978juoqq1jkrwwgfrz3.jpg)

Multiple myeloma - serum protein electrophoresis with M protein




#### Additional testing




Further evaluation for differential diagnoses (guided by clinical features) may include:




* <u>Biochemical evaluation of bone disease</u> (e.g., <u>PTH</u>, <u>vitamin D</u> levels)

* Biochemical evaluation for fatigue and unexplained weight loss (e.g., <u>thyroid function test</u>, <u>diabetes mellitus screening</u>)

* <u>Diagnostic workup for polyneuropathy</u> (e.g., <u>vitamin B12</u> levels, <u>nerve conduction studies</u>)

* <u>Thrombophilia workup</u> (e.g., testing for <u>hereditary thrombophilia</u> or <u>acquired thrombophilias</u>)





### Imaging studies [[5]](/library/M11Mhf0)[[6]](/library/n117hf0)[[10]](/library/fY1ko20)




#### Whole-body <u>low-dose CT</u> (WBLDCT)




* Indications

* First-line test for baseline and follow-up bone surveillance

* More sensitive than <u>x-rays</u> in detecting focal lesions

* Used to guide <u>radiotherapy</u>, <u>biopsies</u>, and <u>surgery</u>

* Findings

* Detection of <u>osteolysis</u> and <u>osteopenia</u>

* Identification of <u>vertebral instability</u> and <u>fracture</u> risk

* <u>Bone marrow</u> <u>plasma cell</u> infiltration in <u>long bones</u>





#### <u>Skeletal survey</u>




Low <u>sensitivity</u>; no longer considered the best initial test




* Indications

* Obtain if other more sensitive techniques are not available.

* May be used to evaluate for <u>skull</u> and <u>rib</u> lesions, which are not well detected by WBLDCT or <u>MRI</u>.

* Findings

* Multiple lytic lesions ("punched-out" holes), e.g., in the <u>skull</u>

* <u>Plasmacytoma</u>

![Osteolytic lesions in multiple myeloma](media/dc2hel4upvxy1j8r0siqmc56.jpg)

#### Ancillary tests




* Indications

* Inconclusive WBLDCT

* Alternative option for baseline and follow-up bone surveillance

* Modalities

* <u>MRI</u> (whole-body or <u>spine</u> and <u>pelvis</u>): highest <u>sensitivity</u> for diffuse <u>bone marrow</u> involvement

* <u>FDG-PET/CT scan</u>: highest <u>sensitivity</u> for extramedullary disease and active lytic bone lesions





### <u>Bone marrow biopsy</u>




* Indication: : <u>confirmatory test</u> indicated for all patients with suspected multiple myeloma

* <u>Fluorescence in situ hybridization</u> (<u>FISH</u>): used for <u>staging of multiple myeloma</u> [[11]](/library/TY16o20)

* High-risk chromosomal abnormalities in multiple myeloma 

* Translocations: t(4;14), t(14;16), t(14;20)

* Others: deletion 17p, gain 1q, <u>p53</u> mutation

* Standard risk abnormalities: t(11;14), t(6;14), <u>trisomies</u>

* <u>Cytology</u>: <u>clusters</u> of <u>plasma cells</u>  

* Mildly organized monoclonal cells

* Perinuclear lucent zone

* Clockface <u>nuclei</u>: <u>Chromatin</u> in the periphery of the <u>nucleus</u> resembles a cartwheel or clock face arrangement.

* Intracytoplasmic crystalline <u>inclusion bodies</u> containing <u>IgG</u>

## Management

### General principles [[5]](/library/M11Mhf0)[[6]](/library/n117hf0)[[7]](/library/Qu1uIi0)[[15]](/library/iu1JIi0)




* Choice of treatment based on:

* Risk <u>stratification</u> (e.g., R-ISS stage)

* Eligibility for <u>autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation</u> (<u>HSCT</u>)

* <u>HSCT</u> eligible: <u>induction chemotherapy</u> followed by <u>autologous HSCT</u>

* <u>HSCT</u> ineligible: <u>chemotherapy</u> alone (e.g., <u>dexamethasone</u> and <u>lenalidomide</u>)

* Goal of therapy: the highest level of remission with the best quality of life

* Prevention and management of complications (e.g., <u>VTE</u>, <u>AKI</u>, bone lesions) is an integral part of treatment.





> [!TIP]
> Refer all patients to a transplant center to determine eligibility for <u>stem cell transplantation</u>.




### <u>Stem cell transplantation</u> [[5]](/library/M11Mhf0)[[6]](/library/n117hf0)[[11]](/library/TY16o20)




* Eligibility: based on <u>performance status</u> (e.g., <u>ECOG</u>, <u>Karnofsky score</u>) and comorbidities

* Process typically includes the following:

* Preparation

* <u>Induction chemotherapy</u> (3–4 cycles)

* <u>Hematopoietic stem cell</u> collection (from peripheral blood)

* <u>Conditioning regimen</u>

* <u>Autologous HSCT</u>

* <u>Maintenance chemotherapy</u>  or <u>consolidation therapy</u> (at least 2 cycles) as an alternative





> [!WARNING]
> Neither advanced age nor poor renal function are <u>absolute contraindications</u> for <u>autologous stem cell transplantation</u>.




> [!TIP]
> <u>Autologous stem cell transplantation</u> improves median overall survival by ∼12 months but is not curative. [[11]](/library/TY16o20)




### <u>Chemotherapy</u> [[5]](/library/M11Mhf0)




There is no expert consensus regarding the optimal chemotherapeutic regimen or number of cycles.




* Transplant eligible patients

* <u>Induction therapy</u>

* Standard risk: (e.g., R-ISS stage I or II) <u>immunomodulator</u> PLUS <u>proteasome inhibitor</u> PLUS <u>steroid</u> (e.g., VRd)

* High risk (e.g., R-ISS stage III): additional <u>cancer immunotherapy</u> (e.g., D-VRd)

* <u>Conditioning regimen</u>: high-dose <u>melphalan</u>

* <u>Maintenance therapy</u>

* Standard risk: <u>lenalidomide</u> monotherapy; <u>bortezomib</u> monotherapy as an alternative

* High risk: <u>proteasome inhibitor</u> with or without <u>lenalidomide</u>

* Transplant ineligible patients: immunomodulators and/or <u>proteasome inhibitors</u> PLUS a <u>steroid</u> (e.g., Rd, VRd)





| <br>Overview of <u>chemotherapeutic agents</u> commonly used for multiple myeloma [[5]](/library/M11Mhf0)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| Medication class | Common agents |
| <u>Proteasome inhibitors</u> | <br><br>* <u>Bortezomib</u> (V)<br><br>* <u>Carfilzomib</u> (K)<br><br>* <u>Ixazomib</u> (I)<br><br><br> |
| Immunomodulators | <br><br>* <u>Lenalidomide</u> (R)<br><br>* <u>Thalidomide</u> (T)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Cancer immunotherapy</u> | <br><br>* <u>Daratumumab</u> (D)<br><br>* Elotuzumab (E)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Steroids</u> | <br><br>* <u>Dexamethasone</u> (d)<br><br>* <u>Prednisone</u> (P)<br><br><br> |
| Alkylators | <br><br>* <u>Melphalan</u> (M)<br><br>* <u>Cyclophosphamide</u> (C)<br><br><br> |
| For the mechanism of action and common adverse effects, see “<u>Chemotherapeutic agents</u>.” |  |





> [!TIP]
> Choice of regimen depends on transplant eligibility, disease <u>risk factors</u> (e.g., R-ISS stage, cytogenetics), patient factors (e.g., <u>frailty</u>, comorbidities, functional status), and patient preferences (e.g., length and quality of life).




### Monitoring [[5]](/library/M11Mhf0)[[11]](/library/TY16o20)[[16]](/library/3Y1SK20)




* Response to treatment

* Defined based on International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG) criteria  [[16]](/library/3Y1SK20)

* Categories range from stringent complete response  to progressive disease

* Clinical relapse

* Defined as recurrence or worsening of <u>myeloma-defining events</u> (e.g., <u>CRAB</u>) after clinical improvement  [[11]](/library/TY16o20)

* Management (i.e., salvage/delayed <u>autologous HSCT</u> and/or <u>chemotherapy</u>) should be individualized.

* After a relapse, therapy may be continued until the disease progresses.





> [!TIP]
> Nearly all patients will relapse; the average time to first relapse is ∼ 3–4 years after initial diagnosis.




### Prevention of complications [[11]](/library/TY16o20)[[17]](/library/uY1pI20)




* Infection prophylaxis

* <u>Recommended immunizations</u>  [[18]](/library/eY1xL20)

* <u>Influenza</u>

* Recombinant zoster

* <u>Haemophilus influenzae</u>

* <u>Pneumococcal vaccines</u>

* <u>Bacteremia</u> and <u>sepsis</u> prophylaxis during the first two cycles of <u>chemotherapy</u>; e.g., <u>levofloxacin</u> (<u>off label</u>) DOSAGE [[11]](/library/TY16o20)[[19]](/library/NY1-620)

* <u>PCP prophylaxis</u> for patients receiving high-dose <u>corticosteroids</u>; e.g., low‑dose <u>TMP/SMX</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Herpes zoster</u> prophylaxis for patients receiving <u>proteasome inhibitors</u>; e.g., <u>valacyclovir</u> (<u>off label</u>) DOSAGE or <u>acyclovir</u> (<u>off label</u>) DOSAGE [[20]](/library/OY1I620)[[21]](/library/lY1v620)

* <u>Prevention of acute kidney injury</u>: e.g., avoid <u>nephrotoxic medications</u>, maintain adequate hydration status

* <u>VTE prophylaxis</u>

* Indicated for all patients, especially those receiving immunomodulatory agents (e.g., <u>lenalidomide</u>)

* The preferred agent (e.g., <u>aspirin</u>, <u>direct oral anticoagulant</u>, <u>LMWH</u>, <u>warfarin</u>) depends on the patient's individual risk of <u>thrombosis</u>.





### Management of complications [[11]](/library/TY16o20)




Management should be provided under specialist guidance.




| Overview of the management of complications of multiple myeloma |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Complication |  | Management options |
| <br>Bone disease [[18]](/library/eY1xL20)[[22]](/library/mY1Vp20)<br> |  | <br><br>* <u>Bisphosphonates</u>: e.g., <u>zoledronic acid</u> (first-line) DOSAGE  [[22]](/library/mY1Vp20)<br><br>* Contraindicated in patients with <u>eGFR</u> < 30 mL/min<br><br>* Recommended for all patients (regardless of the presence of bone lesions on imaging)<br><br>* <u>Denosumab</u> DOSAGE: alternative to <u>bisphosphonates</u>  [[22]](/library/mY1Vp20)<br><br>* <u>Calcium</u> and <u>vitamin D</u> supplementation<br><br>* Recommended for all patients receiving <u>bisphosphonates</u> or <u>denosumab</u> (to prevent <u>hypocalcemia</u>)<br><br>* Start after normalization of serum <u>calcium</u> concentration.<br><br><br> |
| <br>Renal disease [[23]](/library/8Y1OI20)<br> |  | <br><br>* High fluid intake (approx. 3 L/day)<br><br>* Antimyeloma therapy<br><br>* See also “<u>Management of acute kidney injury</u>” and “<u>Management of chronic kidney disease</u>.”<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Peripheral neuropathy</u> [[17]](/library/uY1pI20)<br> |  | <br><br>* Consider <u>pain management</u> with <u>gabapentin</u> or <u>opioid</u> medications.<br><br>* Consider dose reduction or treatment interruption if symptoms worsen in <u>response to chemotherapy</u>.<br><br><br> |
| <br>Hematological complications [[11]](/library/TY16o20)[[17]](/library/uY1pI20)[[18]](/library/eY1xL20)<br> | <u>Anemia</u> | <br><br>* <u>Blood transfusion</u>: Consider for <u>severe anemia</u>.<br><br>* <u>Erythropoietin</u> (<u>EPO</u>): Consider in case of <u>hemoglobin</u> < 10 g/dL during <u>chemotherapy</u>.<br><br><br> |
| <u>Neutropenia</u> | <br>* <u>Granulocyte-colony stimulating factor</u> (<u>G-CSF</u>): if <u>neutrophil</u> count < 1,000/Î¼L<br><br> |  |
| <u>Thrombosis</u> | <br>* See “<u>Treatment of hypercoagulable states</u>.”<br><br> |  |





> [!TIP]
> <u>Treatment of pain</u> (e.g., due to <u>compressive myelopathy</u> or <u>pathological fractures</u>) includes low-dose <u>radiotherapy</u>, high-dose <u>corticosteroids</u>, and invasive therapy (e.g., <u>vertebroplasty</u>, balloon <u>kyphoplasty</u>).




> [!TIP]
> All patients with active multiple myeloma should be treated with <u>bisphosphonates</u> (unless contraindicated), regardless of the presence or absence of imaging findings of bone disease related to multiple myeloma.




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Bisphosphonate</u> therapy and <u>denosumab</u> both increase the risk of <u>osteonecrosis of the jaw</u>. Ensure patients undergo a comprehensive dental evaluation and any necessary dental procedures before starting therapy for bone disease. [[22]](/library/mY1Vp20)

## Differential diagnoses

### Overview of <u>plasma cell dyscrasias</u> (PCDs)




Multiple myeloma should be differentiated from other <u>plasma cell dyscrasias</u>.




| <br>Diagnostic criteria for plasma cell dyscrasias associated with multiple myeloma[[8]](/library/LgXwDx)[[18]](/library/eY1xL20)[[24]](/library/DY11r20)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Plasma cell dyscrasia</u> | Diagnostic criteria |
| <u>Smoldering multiple myeloma</u> | <br><br>* Serum <u>monoclonal protein</u> (<u>IgG</u> or <u>IgA</u>) â¥ 3 g/dL<br><br>* OR urine <u>monoclonal protein</u> â¥ 500 mg/24 h<br><br>* OR 10–60% clonal <u>bone marrow</u> <u>plasma cells</u> in <u>biopsy</u><br><br>* PLUS absence of both <u>myeloma defining events</u> and <u>amyloidosis</u><br><br><br> |
| Solitary <u>plasmacytoma</u> | <br><br>* Presence of a solitary mass (bone or <u>soft tissue</u>) with <u>biopsy</u>-confirmed clonal <u>plasma cells</u><br><br>* PLUS no or minimal <u>bone marrow</u> involvement (< 10% <u>plasma cells</u> in <u>bone marrow</u>)<br><br>* PLUS no evidence of additional bone lesions on imaging<br><br>* PLUS no <u>end-organ damage</u> (i.e., no <u>CRAB criteria</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Plasma cell</u> <u>leukemia</u> | <br><br>* Peripheral blood with either<br><br>* Clonal <u>plasma cells</u> > 2 Ã 10â¹/L<br><br>* OR clonal <u>plasma cells</u> ≥ 20% of <u>leukocytes</u><br><br>* A <u>myeloma-defining event</u> may be present but is not required for diagnosis.<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>POEMS syndrome</u> <br> | <br><br>* <u>Polyneuropathy</u><br><br>* PLUS monoclonal proliferative <u>plasma cell dyscrasia</u><br><br>* PLUS ≥ 1 of the following:<br><br>* Increased serum <u>VEGF</u> (at least 3–4 × <u>ULN</u>)<br><br>* <u>Castleman disease</u><br><br>* Bone lesions (<u>sclerotic</u> or mixed <u>sclerotic</u>/lytic lesion) ≥ 0.8 cm size<br><br>* PLUS ≥ 1 of the following:<br><br>* Organomegaly<br><br>* <u>Signs of hypervolemia</u><br><br>* Endocrinopathy (except <u>diabetes mellitus</u> or <u>hypothyroidism</u>)<br><br>* <u>Skin</u> changes<br><br>* <u>Papilledema</u><br><br>* <u>Thrombocytosis</u> or <u>polycythemia</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance</u> (<u>MGUS</u>) | <br><br>* Paraproteins: monoclonal <u>immunoglobulins</u> (<u>IgG</u> or <u>IgA</u>) detectable in serum < 3 g/dL<br><br>* PLUS < 10% of monoclonal <u>plasma cells</u> in <u>bone marrow</u><br><br>* PLUS no <u>myeloma defining event</u> (i.e., no <u>CRAB criteria</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia</u> [[25]](/library/021eTT0)[[26]](/library/Y21nTT0)<br> | <br><br>* Monoclonal <u>IgM</u> of any concentration detectable on <u>SPEP</u>, <u>UPEP</u>, and/or <u>immunofixation</u><br><br>* PLUS <u>bone marrow biopsy</u> findings of infiltration by small <u>lymphocytes</u> with plasmacytoid or <u>plasma cell</u> differentiation<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> <u>POEMS syndrome</u>: Polyneuropathy, Organomegaly, Endocrinopathy, Monoclonal <u>plasma cell</u> proliferative disorders, Skin changes




### Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (<u>MGUS</u>) [[27]](/library/4UY3Wo)[[28]](/library/kUYmWo)




#### Definition




Characterized by complete or incomplete monoclonal <u>immunoglobulins</u> (of any class) detectable in patient serum without accompanying clinical symptoms




#### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* <u>Prevalence</u>: ∼ 3% in general population ≥ 50 years of age [[29]](/library/q5cCO10)

* The most common type of <u>plasma cell dyscrasia</u> (PCD)





#### Classification




* Non-<u>IgM</u> <u>MGUS</u> (<u>IgG</u>, <u>IgA</u>, <u>IgD</u> <u>MGUS</u>): most common form of <u>MGUS</u> (∼ 55% of cases)

* <u>IgM</u> <u>MGUS</u>: ∼ 15% of cases

* Light-chain <u>MGUS</u> (LC-<u>MGUS</u>)





#### Risk <u>stratification</u> [[30]](/library/p5cLO10)




Patients can be <u>stratified</u> into the following categories according to their risk of progression to multiple myeloma or related <u>malignancy</u>.




* Low-risk <u>MGUS</u> includes all of the following:

* <u>IgG</u> subtype

* <u>M-protein</u> concentration < 1.5 g/dL

* Normal <u>SFLC ratio</u>

* Moderate to high-risk <u>MGUS</u>: any feature not considered low-risk





#### Diagnostics [[30]](/library/p5cLO10)[[31]](/library/N5c-410)[[32]](/library/J5csO10)




* General considerations

* Usually diagnosed as an incidental finding

* Universal screening is not routinely recommended.

* Diagnostic criteria may help establish a diagnosis; see “<u>Diagnostic criteria for plasma cell dyscrasias</u>.”

* Initial studies

* <u>CBC</u>, serum <u>creatinine</u>, and <u>calcium</u>

* <u>SPEP</u> and <u>UPEP</u> with <u>immunofixation</u>

* Quantitative <u>immunoglobulin</u> assessment

* <u>SFLC assay</u>

* Additional studies: usually reserved for patients with moderate to high risk of progression to <u>malignancy</u> or if there is evidence of transformation to another <u>plasma cell dyscrasia</u> (i.e., <u>M-protein</u> concentration â¥ 3 g/dL, findings of a severe PCD) [[31]](/library/N5c-410)

* <u>Bone marrow biopsy</u>

* Skeletal imaging

* WBLDCT (modality of choice)

* A <u>skeletal survey</u> is indicated if CT is not available.

* Whole-body <u>MRI</u> is indicated in patients with inconclusive CT results.





#### Management




* Management is usually expectant.

* Long-term follow up: Monitor for progression to lymphoplasmacytic <u>malignancy</u>.

* Studies: <u>CBC</u>, serum <u>calcium</u> and <u>creatinine</u>, <u>SPEP</u>, and <u>SFLC assays</u>

* Cadence: 6 months after diagnosis and then every 1–3 years.





> [!TIP]
> Monitor patients with <u>MGUS</u> for progression to lymphoplasmacytic <u>malignancy</u>.




#### Complications




* Multiple myeloma

* Transformation of <u>MGUS</u> into multiple myeloma occurs in approx. 1% of cases per year [[31]](/library/N5c-410)

* Typically arises from non-<u>IgM</u> <u>MGUS</u>

* <u>Light chain amyloidosis</u>: can occur with all forms of <u>MGUS</u>

* <u>Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia</u>: only arises from <u>IgM</u> <u>MGUS</u>

* Increased risk of <u>thrombosis</u> (<u>thromboprophylaxis</u> is usually not required) and developing <u>osteoporosis</u> (<u>bone densitometry</u> should be performed at the time of diagnosis)

* <u>Lymphoma</u>





### Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia[[26]](/library/Y21nTT0)




#### Definition




A type of <u>non-Hodgkin</u> <u>lymphoma</u> associated with abnormal production of monoclonal <u>IgM</u> <u>antibodies</u>




#### <u>Epidemiology</u>




Mostly occurs in older adults




#### Clinical features




* <u>Peripheral neuropathy</u>

* Extremities are involved first with progressive, <u>proximal</u>, symmetrical spread

* Presents with <u>paresthesias</u> and <u>weakness</u> (sensory and motor nerve involvement)

* Impaired <u>platelet</u> function → <u>hemorrhagic diathesis</u> with <u>petechial</u> bleeding

* Normochromic <u>anemia</u>

* Formation of <u>cold agglutinins</u> (<u>IgM</u>) with <u>hyperviscosity syndrome</u> 

* <u>Raynaud phenomenon</u>

* Impaired acral blood flow

* <u>Cerebral venous thrombosis</u>

* Impaired <u>vision</u> (e.g., blurry <u>vision</u>)

* <u>Fundoscopic exam</u>

* <u>Retinal hemorrhages</u>

* Dilated, engorged, and segmented retinal <u>veins</u>

* Impaired <u>hearing</u>

* <u>Headaches</u>

* Impaired renal and <u>liver function</u>

* <u>Lymph node</u> enlargement possible

* <u>Constitutional symptoms</u> (e.g., fatigue)





#### Diagnostics [[26]](/library/Y21nTT0)




Diagnostic criteria may help establish a diagnosis; see “<u>Diagnostic criteria for plasma cell dyscrasias</u>.”




* Routine studies

* <u>CBC</u>, <u>CMP</u>

* Increased <u>ESR</u>, <u>uric acid</u>, <u>LDH</u>, and <u>alkaline phosphatase</u>

* Serum <u>β<sub>2</sub> microglobulin</u> level

* <u>Immunoglobulin</u> studies

* <u>SPEP</u> and <u>UPEP</u> with <u>immunofixation</u>

* Quantitative serum <u>immunoglobulin</u> levels

* <u>Bone marrow biopsy</u> and <u>aspirate</u>: ≥ 10% abnormal <u>plasma cells</u> with Dutcher bodies (<u>periodic acid-Schiff</u> positive, <u>cytoplasmic</u> <u>inclusions</u> of <u>IgM</u> deposits that invaginate into the <u>nucleus</u>) [[33]](/library/n217RT0)[[34]](/library/L21wRT0)

* Imaging studies: Consider a <u>contrast-enhanced CT scan</u> of the chest, abdomen, and <u>pelvis</u>.

* Additional studies for suspected <u>hyperviscosity syndrome</u> 

* Serum viscosity measurement

* Ophthalmologic evaluation





> [!NOTE]
> Overproduction of monoclonal IgM suggests Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia rather than multiple myeloma.





#### Treatment




Usually reserved for symptomatic patients




* Targeted treatment: anti-<u>CD20</u> <u>antibodies</u> (e.g., <u>rituximab</u>), <u>Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors</u> (e.g., <u>ibrutinib</u>), <u>purine nucleoside analogs</u> (<u>fludarabine</u> and <u>cladribine</u>), <u>alkylating agents</u> (e.g., <u>cyclophosphamide</u>)

* <u>Hyperviscosity syndrome</u>: <u>plasmapheresis</u>





#### Prognosis




Good, as it is a type of indolent <u>lymphoma</u>




### POEMS syndrome




See “<u>Diagnostic criteria for plasma cell dyscrasias</u>” for details.




* Definition: a rare <u>plasma cell</u> disorder that causes chronic overproduction of <u>proinflammatory cytokines</u>

* Clinical features include:

* <u>Polyneuropathy</u>

* Organomegaly

* Endocrinopathy

* Increased production of monoclonal <u>plasma proteins</u>

* <u>Skin</u> changes





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Complications

### Renal disease




* Dysproteinemia-associated kidney disease [[3]](/library/4kc3Lc0)[[35]](/library/AbXRw9)

* Myeloma cast nephropathy (i.e., <u>myeloma kidney</u>): most common cause of <u>renal injury</u> and <u>renal failure</u> in patients with multiple myeloma

* Clinical features: <u>oliguria</u>, <u>peripheral edema</u>, <u>dyspnea</u>

* Pathophysiology: excessive production and filtration of <u>light chains</u> into the urine → precipitation of <u>light chains</u> in renal tubules → tubular obstruction

* Diagnosis: markedly positive <u>urine sulfosalicylic acid test</u>  and/or <u>urine protein electrophoresis</u>

* May progress to <u>end-stage renal disease</u> (<u>ESRD</u>)

* Monoclonal <u>immunoglobulin</u> deposition disease (MIDD)

* <u>Light chain</u> deposition disease (LCDD)

* <u>Heavy chain</u> deposition disease (HCDD)

* Light and <u>heavy chain</u> deposition disease (LHCDD)

* Type I cryoglobulinemia

* An immune-mediated disorder characterized by the deposition of monoclonal <u>immunoglobulins</u> (<u>IgG</u> and <u>IgM</u>) within <u>blood vessels</u>.

* Most commonly associated with protein-secreting monoclonal gammopathies, including <u>monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance</u>, <u>Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia</u>, and multiple myeloma.

* <u>Type II cryoglobulinemia</u>

* Immunotactoid glomerulopathy

* Proliferative <u>glomerulonephritis</u> with monoclonal <u>immunoglobulin</u> deposits (PGNMID)

* Monoclonal gammopathy-associated <u>C3 glomerulopathy</u>

* Light-chain <u>proximal</u> tubulopathy

* Monoclonal <u>IgM</u>-mediated <u>kidney</u> disease

* Monotypic fibrillary <u>glomerulonephritis</u>

* <u>Hypercalcemia</u>-associated renal damage: leads to <u>hypercalciuria</u> and <u>nephrocalcinosis</u>

* <u>Analgesic nephropathy</u>: caused by long-term intake of <u>NSAIDs</u> for bone <u>pain</u>





![Myeloma cast nephropathy](media/yp0lkwqjgnfo4xtle6lnbhg8.jpg)

Myeloma cast nephropathy




### Systemic manifestations




* <u>AL amyloidosis</u>: <u>Light chains</u> can accumulate as amyloids and may lead to <u>restrictive cardiomyopathy</u>, <u>renal insufficiency</u>, <u>macroglossia</u>, and <u>malabsorption syndromes</u>.

* Infections

* Increased risk due to <u>immunodeficiency</u> (nonfunctional <u>immunoglobulins</u>) and side effects of medications

* Major <u>cause of death</u> in patients with multiple myeloma

* Secondary <u>plasma cell</u> <u>leukemia</u> [[36]](/library/KnaU8O)

* <u>Leukemic</u> course secondary to multiple myeloma

* Diffuse spreading of abnormal cells and distribution of large amounts of <u>plasma cells</u> into the <u>circulatory system</u>

* Rare; occurs in 2–3% of cases

* <u>Hypercalcemic crisis</u>: <u>Osteolysis</u> is associated with chronically elevated <u>calcium</u> levels, which can result in a <u>hypercalcemic crisis</u>.





We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
